questions.prompt: What do words such as stinky and fragrant mainly express in the explanation?

questions.prompt: What does the perfume example show?

evidence.summary: The example illustrates differing subjective reactions to one perfume.

distractors.B: The speaker explicitly says both opposing judgements can be true.

options.label: B

questions.prompt: Which sense is used as a contrast with smell?

options.label: B

tests.title: From smell preferences to shared meanings

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: The ground after {{blank}} produces the smell Georgie calls petrichor.

evidence.summary: Georgie connects the named smell with the ground immediately after rain.

questions.prompt: Neil prefers the smell from a newly opened packet of {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: His example concerns ground coffee rather than the packet as an odour in itself.

questions.prompt: Old books are linked with a {{blank}} feeling about second-hand bookshops.

evidence.summary: The introduction to the bookshop example connects the smell with a sentimental response.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Why can a long list of smell words be misleading about the language's precision?

evidence.summary: The quantity of evaluative labels is distinguished from the ability to describe a smell's specific qualities.

distractors.A: The explanation says the words mainly mean bad-smelling rather than distinct chemical sources.
distractors.B: The list concerns bad smells, while flower comparisons are a separate example.

options.label: A
options.text: Every word in the list refers to a different chemical source.

options.label: B
options.text: The words are all comparisons with pleasant flowers.

options.label: C
options.text: Many of the words repeat a negative evaluation instead of identifying distinct smells.

questions.prompt: What is the perfume example intended to establish?

evidence.summary: Different subjective reactions can both be valid descriptions of the speakers' experience.

distractors.A: The example concerns evaluation rather than a physical change in the smell.
distractors.C: The example explicitly concerns one perfume judged by different people.

options.label: A
options.text: A change in the adjective proves that the smell has changed physically.

options.label: B
options.text: Opposing personal evaluations can coexist without one being objectively false.

options.label: C
options.text: Using two adjectives proves that there are two different perfumes.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the taste examples in the researcher's account?

evidence.summary: Taste terms are presented as producing common ideas unlike subjective smell evaluations.

distractors.B: The contrast concerns shared qualities such as salty rather than just liking.
distractors.C: Age is introduced later with children's curiosity, not as this contrast.

options.label: A
options.text: They evoke a more commonly agreed description than the smell labels.

options.label: B
options.text: They describe only whether the speaker likes the food.

options.label: C
options.text: They depend on the age of the person speaking.

tests.title: Smell descriptions: scope and subjective evidence

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which material illustrates Georgie's liking before she mentions rain? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Her first preference is the smell of leather, before the stronger preference for rain.

questions.prompt: What contents make the newly opened packet appealing to Neil? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The packet's ground coffee, rather than the packaging itself, supplies the liked smell.

questions.prompt: What feeling is associated with old books and second-hand bookshops? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The example links old-book smells with a sentimental feeling about bookshops.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which distinction underlies the criticism of the long vocabulary list?

evidence.summary: The argument separates the number of negative labels from the specificity of the descriptions they provide.

distractors.A: The reliance on comparisons is contrasted with the scarcity of dedicated smell terms.
distractors.C: The claim concerns vocabulary precision, not an inability to perceive differences.

options.label: A
options.text: Object comparisons establish that every smell has its own dedicated adjective.

options.label: B
options.text: Many ways to express dislike do not necessarily identify many distinct odour qualities.

options.label: C
options.text: A short list proves that nobody can notice differences between smells.

questions.prompt: Why can fragrant and stinky both be true in the perfume example?

evidence.summary: The two speakers can disagree in their reaction without either reaction misreporting that person's experience.

distractors.B: The example does not analyse ingredients or require two substances.
distractors.C: The adjectives retain opposite evaluations; subjectivity explains their coexistence.

options.label: A
options.text: They report different personal evaluations rather than mutually exclusive objective properties.

options.label: B
options.text: The researcher establishes that perfume contains two separate substances.

options.label: C
options.text: The adjectives are defined as having exactly the same meaning.

questions.prompt: What limitation remains even after someone says the perfume is fragrant?

evidence.summary: The label communicates evaluation without specifying the smell's distinctive qualities.

distractors.A: Fragrant communicates a positive evaluation in the explanation.
distractors.B: Taste is a comparison between senses, not a property attributed to this perfume.

options.label: A
options.text: The listener cannot tell whether the speaker's evaluation is positive.

options.label: B
options.text: The listener has been told that the perfume must taste sweet.

options.label: C
options.text: The listener still lacks a specific description of the perfume's actual smell.

questions.prompt: Which statement would overstate the suggested role of upbringing?

evidence.summary: A tentative upbringing explanation is not proof of a universal cause across societies.

distractors.A: The tentative maybe is consistent with a possible explanation rather than proof.
distractors.B: The parent stopping discussion is an example actually reported.

options.label: B

questions.prompt: Which conclusion keeps the distinction made about English vocabulary?

distractors.A: The point is the shortage of precise quality terms despite numerous negative labels.
distractors.C: The programme has already given many smell-related words.
